title: Mind the Gap: Data Completeness and Federated Medical AI for Equitable Transplant Optimization
content: Medical artificial intelligence increasingly depends on collaboration across distributed healthcare data environments, yet model performance, fairness, and interpretability remain constrained by the completeness of the decision-relevant information available for learning. This study examines that problem in organ transplantation, a time-critical, interorganizational healthcare supply chain in which transplant centers, clinicians, laboratories, and coordinating institutions possess different elements of patient and allocation information. Using publicly reported Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network and Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients data, we present a retrospective descriptive case study of policy changes correcting race-inclusive estimated glomerular filtration rate calculations in kidney allocation. The deceased-donor kidney transplant rate among Black adult waitlisted candidates increased from 20.8 per 100 patient-years in 2021 to 26.1 in 2023 and 26.5 in 2024; 14,701 waiting-time modifications restored a median 1.7 years of waiting time to affected registrations. Although aggregate observational data preclude causal attribution, the case illustrates how deficiencies in decision-relevant information can have measurable implications for equitable organ allocation. We argue that federated medical AI offers a promising architecture for learning across distributed clinical data while preserving institutional data stewardship, privacy, and human oversight. Data completeness must therefore accompany privacy-preserving collaboration if federated AI is to support equitable transplant optimization.
